title: Blood cultures
summary: Sterile collection of blood for bacterial culture in suspected sepsis, bacteraemia, endocarditis, and fever assessment.
indications: Fever with systemic illness or signs of sepsis
Fever with cardiac murmur or prosthetic valve (endocarditis risk)
Fever with intravenous line or recent invasive procedure
Community-acquired pneumonia with severe systemic illness
Fever in patient with intra-abdominal infection
contraindications: None absolute; proceed even if bleeding tendency present (importance of culture outweighs bleeding risk)
precautions: Strict aseptic technique essential: contamination is leading cause of misinterpretation
Collect before antibiotics if possible; never delay antibiotics for culture in septic shock
Collect at least 2 sets from different sites to distinguish contamination from true bacteraemia
Use appropriate blood volume (10 mL per bottle for adults; 1–3 mL for children)
Do not touch needle or culture bottle sterile field after site preparation
equipment: Sterile blood culture bottles (aerobic and anaerobic sets; minimum 2 sets)
Sterile vacutainer system (if using vacuum collection)
Alcohol preparation swabs (70% isopropyl alcohol or chlorhexidine)
preparation: Explain procedure to patient: brief needle insertion for blood sample, important for diagnosing serious infection
Choose peripheral vein (arm preferred; femoral vein acceptable if necessary)
Position patient comfortably; have assistant available if needed
Gather all equipment before beginning (minimises need to interrupt sterile procedure)
Explain that results take 24–48 hours (or up to 5 days for fastidious organisms)

steps.title: Site preparation
steps.instruction: Don sterile gloves. Clean venipuncture site with 70% isopropyl alcohol or chlorhexidine swab using firm circular motion for 30 seconds. Allow to air dry completely (critical for disinfection). Do not re-palpate site after cleaning.
cautions: Inadequate drying time reduces disinfection efficacy—allow full 30 seconds
Re-palpating site introduces bacteria; avoid this step
tips: Use chlorhexidine for better disinfection than alcohol alone
Let site air dry rather than wiping—faster and more effective

steps.title: Culture bottle preparation
steps.instruction: Clean rubber septum of culture bottles with alcohol swab and allow to dry. Have aerobic and anaerobic bottles ready. For each set, insert needle into aerobic bottle first (to avoid air in anaerobic bottle), then anaerobic bottle.
cautions: Air in anaerobic bottle causes contamination—inoculate aerobic first
Do not touch bottle septum after cleaning
tips: Prepare bottles before venipuncture to minimise time between draw and inoculation
Label bottles immediately before puncturing—prevents mix-up

steps.title: Venepuncture
steps.instruction: Using sterile technique, insert needle into vein at 15–30° angle. Obtain 10 mL blood in adults (scalp vein in neonates: 0.5–1 mL, as tolerated). Withdraw needle and apply gentle pressure with sterile gauze.
cautions: Deep vein puncture increases contamination risk—use appropriate angle
Multiple attempts increase contamination—consider ultrasound guidance if difficult
tips: Stabilise vein with non-dominant hand to prevent movement
Use butterfly needle or smaller gauge (25G) for difficult veins if needed

steps.title: Inoculation of culture bottles
steps.instruction: Using same syringe and needle (or transfer needle), fill aerobic bottle first, then anaerobic bottle with 5–10 mL per bottle. Ensure needle penetrates rubber septum; do not introduce air into bottles. Mix gently by inversion 8–10 times.
cautions: Do not introduce air into anaerobic bottle—defeats purpose of anaerobic culture
Wrong volume in bottles (too little) reduces culture sensitivity
tips: Change needle between venipuncture and bottle inoculation if equipment allows—reduces contamination
Fill bottles to appropriate line if marked; follow bottle instructions for volume

steps.title: Repeat collection (second set)
steps.instruction: Repeat entire process (site re-preparation, venepuncture from different site) to obtain second set of bottles within 1 hour. This is critical to differentiate true bacteraemia from contamination (same organism in 2+ sets = bacteraemia; different organisms = contamination).
cautions: Single set collection reduces diagnostic value—two sets mandatory for interpretation
Different sites reduce contamination risk—do not use same site twice
tips: Document site of each collection (e.g., 'left AC', 'right wrist') for interpretation
If unable to obtain two sets, document reason in medical record

steps.title: Labelling and documentation
steps.instruction: Label each set immediately with patient name, date, time, and source site. Document in patient record. Record indication for culture and whether antibiotics given (and when). Send to microbiology lab immediately (within 2 hours at room temperature).
cautions: Delay in transport reduces organism recovery—bacteria may die or contaminants overgrow
Do not refrigerate cultures—kills some organisms (Haemophilus, Neisseria)
tips: Transport at room temperature in dedicated culture carrier if available
Flag culture bottles if sepsis suspected—lab will prioritise processing

complications: Needle-stick injury (occupational exposure)—standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis if required
Local infiltration or haematoma—rare if good technique; apply pressure if occurs
Vasovagal syncope—ask patient to lie flat if dizzy; rare with experienced operator
Contamination (most common)—distinguished from true growth by different organisms in different sets
troubleshooting: Difficult venipuncture: Use ultrasound guidance if available; consider central line sampling only if absolutely necessary
Single set only collected: Document reason; interpret cautiously; consider repeat collection if clinical suspicion remains
Bottles filled with insufficient blood: May reduce sensitivity; document for lab interpretation
Delay in transport (>2 hours): Organism may die (especially Haemophilus); bacterial overgrowth of contaminants may occur
aftercare: Apply pressure to puncture site with gauze for 2–3 minutes; advise patient to keep arm straight
Provide patient with result timeline (cultures typically read at 24 hours; negative results at 48 hours)
Once culture grows organism: review sensitivities and adjust antibiotics if needed (de-escalate if contaminant)
In negative cultures with high clinical suspicion: discuss with microbiology; consider repeat culture
documentation: Record date and time of collection
Document site(s) where blood drawn (essential for contamination assessment)
Record number of sets obtained (must be ≥2 for reliable interpretation)
Note whether antibiotics given before or after culture
Record indication for culture (fever, suspected endocarditis, etc.)
Document culture results: organism, antimicrobial sensitivities, interpretation (true bacteraemia vs contamination)
escalation: Fever with positive blood cultures (same organism in ≥2 sets): presumed bacteraemia/sepsis—continue antibiotics, review sensitivities, consider source control
Fever with negative blood cultures but high clinical suspicion: consider repeat cultures, specialist imaging, or other diagnoses
Contamination (different organisms): reassess clinical status; repeat culture if sepsis remains suspected
Slow-growing organisms: notify lab of clinical suspicion; extend incubation period
competency: Trained in aseptic venipuncture technique with minimal contamination
Understands importance of 2+ sets and different sites for contamination detection
Able to inoculate culture bottles without introducing air bubbles
Knows indications for blood culture and interpretation of positive vs contaminated results
Familiar with standard precautions and needle-stick management
